props.title: Victory at Entebbe

sections.content: Victory at Entebbe launched a wave of urgent, ripped-from-the-headlines terrorism films that included Raid on Entebbe (1977) and Operation Thunderbolt (1977). All three films dramatized Israel's daring July 1976 rescue mission of hijacked Air France passengers held at Uganda's Entebbe Airport. The made-for-TV Victory at Entebbe got there first, rushing to air within months of the actual events with an all-star cast including Anthony Hopkins, Burt Lancaster, and Elizabeth Taylor. The film established the template for dramatizing modern counter-terrorism operations that influenced later films like Munich (2005) and Zero Dark Thirty (2012).

sections.content: The rush to dramatize Entebbe sparked a unique moment where three major productions tackled the same events from different angles. While Victory at Entebbe emphasized the hostage drama and international diplomacy, Raid on Entebbe (1977) focused more on military tactics, and Operation Thunderbolt (1977) provided the Israeli perspective. This multi-lens approach to a single incident presaged how modern events like the hunt for Bin Laden would be depicted across films like Zero Dark Thirty (2012), SEAL Team Six (2012) and Code Name: Geronimo (2012). SUBHEAD: Evolution of Aviation Terrorism Films

The Entebbe films marked a crucial shift in how terrorism was portrayed on screen. Earlier hijacking films like Skyjacked (1972) treated air piracy more like traditional crime dramas. Post-Entebbe, films like Delta Force (1986) and Executive Decision (1996) emphasized the political and military response to terrorism. This evolution culminated in post-9/11 films like United 93 (2006) and Flight 93 (2006), which like the Entebbe trilogy, offered different perspectives on the same tragic events.
